title: Project Overview
description: Kachabity is a storefront for handcrafted Tunisian products plus a full back office (orders, stock, CRM, point of sale, purchasing, accounting). CLAUDE.md is the real map of the project: it explains that the Next.js 15 site renders pages while every /api request is served by a separate NestJS API on plain Postgres. The README is create-next-app boilerplate, so start here instead.

title: Site Shell and Locales
description: The root layout sets fonts, metadata and the html lang from the x-locale header, while the locale layout renders the header, footer and cart drawer once for every storefront page under app/[locale]. language-utils defines the three locales (en, fr, ar) with Arabic as the RTL default, which is why RTL is applied per section rather than globally.
languageLesson: Next.js App Router layouts nest by folder: app/layout.tsx wraps everything, and app/[locale]/layout.tsx wraps only routes under the dynamic [locale] segment, receiving the locale as a route param.

title: Middleware: The Front Gate
description: Before any page renders, middleware.ts redirects unlocalized paths to a detected locale, refreshes expired sessions, and gates /admin pages by role and permission. The role model it relies on (owner, admin, staff and the PERMISSIONS list) lives in lib/admin-auth.ts, and the session cookies are signed and verified locally through lib/auth-session.ts, so no network call is needed on most requests.

title: From Page to API
description: next.config.ts rewrites every /api/* request to the NestJS server at NEST_URL, so the browser never talks to the database. Storefront pages read public data through lib/storefront-api.ts (server-side via NEST_URL, browser-side via the rewrite), and lib/catalog-cache.ts wraps those reads in a tagged Next.js data cache that admin writes invalidate. The home page shows this pattern: it loads cached data on the server and passes it down as initial props.

title: NestJS API Bootstrap
description: On the other side of the rewrite, api/src/main.ts starts the NestJS app and app.module.ts wires every controller, the database module, the global auth guard and the error filter. It has the highest fan-out in the graph, so it is the best index of what the API offers. api/src/common/api.ts provides the shared plumbing: the response envelope, ApiError, and mapping of zod and database errors to clean 4xx responses.
languageLesson: NestJS modules use decorators (@Module, @Controller, @Injectable) to declare dependency injection: providers listed in a module are constructed once and injected into constructors that ask for them by type.

title: Access Control on Every Route
description: The global auth guard enforces two rule sources together: decorators on each route (@Public, @Requires, @AdminOnly, @OwnerOnly) and the path-based table in lib/api-access.ts, which is shared with the Next.js side. A route with neither is denied by default, and refused calls are logged, building on the role model from Step 3. Accounts, sign-in, refresh and password resets are handled by the auth controller with bcrypt hashes and revocable session rows.

title: Database Access Layer
description: api/src/db/database.ts is the most depended-on API file: it runs Kysely on pg as the table owner, offers withActor transactions that tag writes for the activity log, and db.call for invoking Postgres functions with named arguments. embed.ts builds JSON embeds that filter soft-deleted rows, reflecting the project rule that nothing is hard-deleted and every read must check deleted_at.

title: Schema and Transactional Writes
description: supabase/migrations is the schema source of truth. The storefront rebuild migration defines the core tables (products, variants, orders, site settings), and the transactional-writes migration moves multi-row operations like create_order and save_product into Postgres functions so they succeed or fail as a whole. This is why the API calls db.call() from Step 7 instead of chaining several inserts, and why the soft-delete migration matters for every read.
languageLesson: Wrapping related writes in a PL/pgSQL function makes them atomic: the function body runs inside the caller's transaction, so any raised exception rolls back every row it touched.

title: Cart, Checkout and Pricing
description: The cart lives only in the browser (localStorage), and the checkout page submits it through lib/orders.ts to POST /api/orders. The orders controller never trusts client amounts: priceOrder() in commerce.ts re-prices every line with active discounts, shipping and tax, and returns 409 codes such as PRICES_CHANGED when they differ. Any change to how the storefront computes a price must be mirrored here.

title: Stock as Movements
description: Stock is never written directly: every change is an append-only stock_movements row, and a database trigger updates inventory_levels per variant and location, rejecting negative stock. The stock controllers record movements, and lib/stock.ts turns trigger errors like insufficient_stock into readable messages. Order status changes from Step 9 deduct or restore stock through the same mechanism.

title: Colissimo Delivery
description: Validating an order creates a Colissimo parcel through lib/colissimo.ts, which wraps the carrier's v1 parcel API and v2 tracking and editing API. The delivery controller sends, edits and hands over parcels, and the tracking service polls every 15 minutes, marking orders shipped, delivered or returned and recording cash the carrier still owes. The deliveries table is the parcel list because the carrier API cannot list an account's parcels.

title: The Admin Back Office
description: The admin is a client-rendered Ant Design dashboard whose layout builds a sidebar filtered by the permissions from Step 3. lib/admin-i18n.tsx, the most imported file in the project, gives every screen its EN/FR/AR text through useAdminT, and the role context exposes can(permission) to hide controls. ERP screens share erp-client.ts for API calls, while real enforcement stays in the API guard from Step 6.

title: ERP: Money and Accounting
description: The ERP migrations add the CRM, payments, point of sale, purchasing and Tunisian-standard accounting. Payments are separate from delivery: order_payments rows drive each order's paid status, and triggers book journal entries for delivered sales, payments and bills. The finance controllers expose reports such as the trial balance and VAT summary on top of these functions.

title: Real-Time Notifications
description: Database triggers write notification rows for new orders and owner alerts, then announce them on a Postgres channel. The notification-events service LISTENs on that channel, streams rows to open admin tabs over server-sent events, and sends Web Push to subscribed browsers, tying the database logic from earlier steps to the admin UI.

title: Build, CI and Deployment
description: The site deploys on Vercel while the API runs on one AWS EC2 server defined in Terraform (aws.tf), alongside Postgres, Caddy, S3 buckets and a budget alert. The API image comes from api/Dockerfile and runs under deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml. GitHub Actions run ci.yml on pull requests and deploy.yml on pushes to main, deploying the API only when it changed; docs/DEPLOY.md walks through the whole setup.
languageLesson: Terraform resources declare desired state; terraform plan previews the diff against the state file before apply changes real infrastructure. GitHub Actions jobs can depend on each other with needs, so a deploy job runs only after CI passes.
